author: ishvarakrishna
period: Commonly placed around the 4th–5th century CE; dates are approximate
summary: The earliest surviving systematic text of Sankhya: about seventy verses on purusha, prakriti, the three gunas and the 25 principles.
whyRead: Sankhya supplies the vocabulary of gunas, prakriti and purusha that runs through the Gita, Yoga and the Puranas. This short text is the clearest classical statement of that dualist system.
questions: What is the relation of consciousness to matter?
Why do we suffer, and can suffering end for good?
What are the basic principles (tattvas) of reality?

keyTeachings.title: The problem of threefold suffering
keyTeachings.text: The text begins from suffering in three forms, from oneself, from other beings and from natural or cosmic forces, and seeks a remedy more lasting than ordinary or ritual means.

keyTeachings.title: Purusha and prakriti
keyTeachings.text: Reality has two irreducible kinds: many conscious but inactive purushas, and a single, unconscious but active prakriti (primal nature). Experience arises from their proximity.

keyTeachings.title: The three gunas
keyTeachings.text: Prakriti consists of three gunas: sattva (clarity, lightness), rajas (activity, passion) and tamas (inertia, heaviness). Their balance and imbalance explain the variety of the world and of minds.

keyTeachings.title: The 25 tattvas
keyTeachings.text: From prakriti evolve intellect (buddhi or mahat), the I-maker (ahankara), mind (manas), five senses of knowing, five organs of action, five subtle elements and five gross elements. With purusha these make 25 principles.

keyTeachings.title: Effects pre-exist in their cause
keyTeachings.text: Sankhya holds satkaryavada: an effect already exists in potential form in its material cause. This underwrites its account of the world as an unfolding of prakriti.

keyTeachings.title: Bondage and liberation through discrimination
keyTeachings.text: Bondage is the failure to distinguish purusha from prakriti. Liberation (kaivalya) comes through discriminating knowledge of their difference, after which prakriti ceases to act for that purusha.

structure.label: About 72 verses (karikas)
structure.note: The count in the received text is around 72; the final verses describe the transmission of the teaching

passages.about: The threefold suffering and the inquiry into its removal

relatedTexts.note: Yoga adopts Sankhya metaphysics and adds Ishvara and a meditative method
The Gita uses Sankhya terms, for instance the gunas in chapter 14 and prakriti and purusha in chapter 13
Vedanta commentators argue against Sankhya's independent prakriti
